items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the civil service law, in relation to enacting the "state workforce injury reduction act"
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S2842

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the civil service law, in relation to enacting the
"state workforce injury reduction act"

PURPOSE OF BILL:

To ensure that agencies seriously examine injuries to their employees
and formulate ways to prevent similar injuries from occurring in the
future.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill names the act the "state workforce injury
reduction act".

Section 2 of the bill amends section 7 of the civil service law by
adding a new subdivision 7 that requires each state agency referenced
in the annual report issued by the president of the civil service
commission pursuant to this section to write and submit an action plan
with participation from employee representatives for reducing
occurrences of such injuries in the coming year.

Section 3 requires the act to take effect immediately.

JUSTIFICATION:

Currently the president of the New York State Department of Civil
Service produces an annual report describing occupational injuries,
illnesses, and workers' compensation claims for each state agency.
However, there is no requirement that agencies respond to the report
with a plan for reducing the kinds of injuries identified in the
report. This legislation would ensure that agencies work with employee
representatives to seriously examine injuries to their employees and
formulate ways to prevent similar injuries from occurring in the
future.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2013-1014: S. 1934 - Referred to Civil Services & Pension Committee.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

Minimal costs, but less worker compensation claims as a result of the
passage of this legislation will result in savings to New York State.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect immediately.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 267

TO THE SENATE:

I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:

Senate Bill Number 2842-A, entitled:

    "AN  ACT to amend the civil service law, in relation to enacting the
      state workforce injury reduction act"

    NOT APPROVED

  Currently, the President of the Civil Service Commission  is  required
to  prepare an Annual Report detailing injuries, illnesses, and workers'
compensation experiences for all State agencies. This bill would require
each identified agency, for the first time,  to  prepare  and  submit  a
"written  action  plan" for reducing injuries within 90 days of publica-
tion of the Annual Report.

  There is no doubt that the State, like  any  employer,  should  always
strive  to  reduce the number of workplace injuries. For this reason, my
Administration  implemented  a  Workers'  Compensation  Taskforce  Pilot
Program  in  2015  to identify how we can better prevent workforce acci-
dents, provide better medical case management and claims servicing, help
individuals get back to work sooner, and reduce fraud and abuse  in  the
system.  In  addition  to  this Taskforce, the State and its unions have
previously negotiated  health  and  safety  labor-management  committees
tasked  with  studying  and reporting on health and safety issues. These
committees provide a mechanism for the proactive development and  imple-
mentation  of  health and safety measures at the various locations where
employees work. Additionally, there are specific and  separate  Workers'
Compensation  labor-management committees, which, among other tasks, are
charged with focusing on workplace injuries and  absences  in  order  to
develop prevention strategies to reduce or eliminate the risk of on-the-
job injury.

  This bill, while laudable, undermines these efforts by implementing an
unfunded  mandate.  Requiring  every  agency,  department, and authority
listed in the Annual Report to submit a written action plan would  place
a  significant  strain  on  these  entities,  without  any  appropriated
resources. In addition to the costs and administrative  burdens  to  the
agencies,  the bill would require the agencies to rush to decisions when
a more measured and systemic review of the important issue of  workplace
safety  is  warranted.  Furthermore,  requiring  the  action plans to be
completed within 90 days would result in less effective, more  haphazard
plans that would not accomplish the policy goals of this bill.

  For  these reasons, I am therefore constrained to veto this bill. I am
directing the various stakeholders to communicate with my staff so  that
we  can  assess  their  concerns and incorporate their feedback into the
extensive work currently underway to improve workplace safety.

  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
